title: HE DIDN’T JUST STEAL HIS FATHER’S THRONE. HE TOOK HIS FATHER’S WOMEN—AND MADE ALL ISRAEL WATCH.
paragraphs: HE DIDN’T JUST STEAL HIS FATHER’S THRONE. HE TOOK HIS FATHER’S WOMEN—AND MADE ALL ISRAEL WATCH.

Why did Absalom’s adviser command something so shocking? The disturbing truth behind 2 Samuel 16:20–22 reveals how sexual humiliation became a weapon of political power—and why the story ultimately points us to a King who conquers not by disgracing others, but by bearing our disgrace Himself.
There are sins committed in darkness.
And then there are sins deliberately dragged into the sunlight because someone wants the whole world to see.
What happened on the rooftop of King David’s palace was not a secret affair. It was not a moment of uncontrollable passion. It was not even primarily about sexual desire.
It was a calculated political act.
A son wanted his father's kingdom.
An adviser knew exactly how to make reconciliation almost impossible.
And ten women, whose names Scripture does not even record, were caught in the middle of a brutal struggle for power.
But here is what makes this story even more disturbing.
Years earlier, another man had stood on a rooftop in Jerusalem, looked upon a woman, and used royal power to take what was not his.
That man was David.
Now David's own son was standing at the center of a public sexual scandal in the very palace his father had abandoned.
Coincidence?
Not according to the biblical narrative.
And before we finish, you may discover that the most frightening thing about this story is not simply what Absalom did to his father.
It is what happens when human beings become so desperate for control that they stop seeing other people as people.
Because the moment power becomes your god, someone else usually becomes your sacrifice.
And that is where this story begins.
Absalom was not an ordinary rebellious son.
He was handsome, charismatic, politically gifted, and deeply wounded by the dysfunction of his father's household.

His sister Tamar had been sexually violated by their half brother Amnon. David became angry, but the biblical account records no corresponding punishment of Amnon. Absalom eventually murdered Amnon and fled.
Years passed.
The family never truly healed.
And resentment became something far more dangerous.
A political ambition.

Absalom began cultivating public loyalty. He positioned himself near the city gate, listened to people's grievances, questioned whether they would receive justice, and presented himself as the leader who would finally care about them.
Second Samuel 15:6 describes the result:
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” (KJV)
Notice the language.
He did not begin by taking the throne.
He began by taking hearts.
That is often how destructive leadership works.

It offers understanding before demanding allegiance. It presents itself as the answer to every disappointment. It convinces wounded people that their pain can be healed by putting someone new in power.
And sometimes, by the time people recognize the manipulation, they have already surrendered their judgment.
Eventually, Absalom declared himself king.
David fled Jerusalem.
The father who once defeated Goliath was now running from his own son.
Imagine that journey.
The king leaving his city.
The palace behind him.
The sound of weeping.
The humiliation of watching his own household collapse.
David had conquered enemies on battlefields, but he could not command his broken family to become whole.
Then Absalom entered Jerusalem.
And he turned to a man named Ahithophel.
Ahithophel was no ordinary political adviser.
Second Samuel 16:23 says that his counsel was regarded in those days with extraordinary authority, as though someone had consulted the word of God.
That description explains his influence. It does not mean that his advice was morally approved by God.
A person can possess remarkable intelligence and still use it for devastating evil.
A person can understand politics and completely misunderstand righteousness.
A person can give advice that works and still lead someone toward destruction.
Absalom asked:
“Give counsel among you what we shall do.” (2 Samuel 16:20, KJV)
Ahithophel's response was chilling.

“Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.” (2 Samuel 16:21, KJV)
Read that carefully.
Ahithophel was not recommending romance.
He was recommending a public act of sexual domination.
He wanted Absalom to take the women associated with David's royal household, making a visible declaration that David's authority had been replaced.
In the ancient royal world, access to a king's women could carry political significance because the royal household was closely associated with the king's position.
We see this connection elsewhere in Scripture.
When Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine, Genesis 35:22 recorded the offense, and Genesis 49:3–4 later connected Reuben's sexual misconduct with the loss of his preeminence.

In 1 Kings 2:13–25, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag, who had attended David in his old age, was interpreted by Solomon as a threat connected to the kingdom, even though 1 Kings 1:4 explicitly states that David had not had sexual relations with her.
These passages do not make every case identical.
But they reveal a recurring political reality.
A king's household was not treated as an entirely private sphere.
Claims involving women associated with the royal household could be interpreted as claims involving royal succession.
Ahithophel understood this.
And he wanted Absalom's rebellion to become unmistakable.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:21 makes his reasoning particularly revealing.
וְשָׁמַע כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי־נִבְאַשְׁתָּ אֶת־אָבִיךָ
Ve-shama kol-Yisra'el ki-niv'ashta et-avikha.
A close rendering is:
“And all Israel will hear that you have become odious to your father.”
The Hebrew verb translated “become odious” conveys the idea of becoming offensive, detestable, or repugnant.
Ahithophel wanted the nation to know that Absalom had crossed a line so grievous that ordinary father-son reconciliation would appear impossible.
Why?
Because rebellion becomes unstable when followers suspect their leader might negotiate peace and abandon them.
Ahithophel wanted to remove that uncertainty.
He wanted Absalom's supporters to believe there was no turning back.
The final words of his counsel explain the political objective:
“Then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.”
Strengthened hands meant strengthened resolve.
His supporters would become more confident that Absalom was committed to overthrowing David.
In other words, Ahithophel was saying:
Make your rebellion so public, so offensive, and so irreversible that everyone knows you have chosen the throne over your father.
And Absalom listened.
Second Samuel 16:22 records:
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.” (KJV)
A tent.
A rooftop.
A public announcement through an act of sexual possession.

The text does not require us to imagine the entire population literally watching the sexual acts themselves. The tent and the phrase “in the sight of all Israel” emphasize the public, notorious character of what Absalom did.
It was meant to be known.
It was meant to humiliate David.
It was meant to announce a transfer of power.
But we must not miss the people whom political readings often leave behind.
The women.
David had left ten concubines to keep the palace when he fled, according to 2 Samuel 15:16.
These women did not design Absalom's rebellion.
They did not appoint Ahithophel.
They did not choose the political struggle consuming Jerusalem.
Yet their bodies became the instruments through which powerful men communicated dominance.
Scripture does not tell us their private thoughts or describe their individual responses. We should not invent details about what each woman experienced.
But neither should we romanticize their situation.
The narrative presents them within a severe imbalance of power, subjected to an act orchestrated for political humiliation.
They were not merely symbols in a royal dispute.
They were human beings.
And the tragedy did not end on the rooftop.

After David returned to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us that he placed these ten women in a guarded house, provided for them, and did not resume marital relations with them. They lived in confinement until their deaths, described as living in widowhood.
The rebellion ended.
But their lives were never restored to what they had been.
That detail should trouble us.
Because sometimes history remembers the names of kings while barely acknowledging the suffering of those crushed beneath their decisions.
And sometimes people who never started a conflict carry its consequences for the rest of their lives.
Perhaps that is the part of this story you recognize.
Not the throne.
Not the palace.
But the feeling of being caught in somebody else's war.
A family dispute you did not create.
A betrayal you did not deserve.
A relationship where someone treated your dignity as expendable.
A powerful person making decisions while you were left to live with the damage.
The Bible does not call such cruelty good simply because it appears in the story of Israel's kings.
Describing evil is not endorsing evil.
And the God who inspired Scripture does not require us to pretend that the suffering of vulnerable people is insignificant.
But there is another layer to this passage.
One that takes us back to David's own sin.
Years earlier, in 2 Samuel 11, David had been on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba bathing.
He sent messengers.
He took her.
And after she became pregnant, he attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his schemes failed, David arranged for her husband Uriah to be placed in deadly battle conditions.
Uriah died.
David then took Bathsheba as his wife.
For a time, the king appeared to have successfully managed the scandal.
But 2 Samuel 11:27 ends with a devastating judgment:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” (KJV)
What the palace could conceal, God could see.
What political power could excuse, God condemned.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
And in 2 Samuel 12:11–12, Nathan announced that calamity would arise against David from his own household and that his wives would be taken in public view.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 is striking:
כִּי אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר וַאֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Ki attah asita va-sater, va-ani e'eseh et-ha-davar hazzeh neged kol-Yisra'el ve-neged ha-shamesh.
A close translation is:
“For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.”
Secretly.
Before all Israel.
Before the sun.
The contrast is deliberate.
David's abuse of power had been concealed.
The humiliation that entered his household would become public.
The rooftop scene in 2 Samuel 16 is therefore not merely a random political scandal.
It is a narrative fulfillment of Nathan's prophetic warning.
But we must handle that truth carefully.
God's announcement of judgment does not mean that Absalom's actions were morally righteous, that Ahithophel's counsel was holy, or that the women deserved what happened to them.
The Bible can describe God sovereignly bringing judgment through human events while still holding the human participants accountable for their evil.
Absalom remained responsible for his rebellion.
Ahithophel remained responsible for his counsel.
And the women must never be blamed for David's earlier sin.
This distinction matters because careless interpretations can turn Scripture into a weapon against victims.
The prophetic warning explains the theological significance of the event.
It does not justify the abuse.
And here is the painful lesson.
David had been forgiven, but forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence of what he had done.
When David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD,” Nathan answered in 2 Samuel 12:13:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.” (KJV)
That was real mercy.
Real forgiveness.
But the chapter also records continuing judgment and grief.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened.
Grace does not require victims to deny their wounds.
Repentance does not guarantee that broken trust immediately returns.
And a forgiven sinner may still need to face consequences, repair what can be repaired, and accept responsibility for damage that cannot simply be undone.
That is not the absence of grace.
It is the seriousness of sin.
Perhaps you have prayed for forgiveness over something that still haunts you.
Perhaps God has been merciful, yet the consequences remain.
A relationship has changed.
A child no longer trusts you.
A marriage is struggling.
A decision made years ago continues to affect your family.
And you wonder whether the presence of consequences means the absence of God's mercy.
David's story says otherwise.
But it also refuses to make repentance cheap.
The grace of God is not permission to keep harming people.
It is the mercy that calls us to turn from sin and walk in truth.
Now look again at Absalom.
He wanted the kingdom.
He wanted recognition.
He wanted the people to believe he was the rightful answer to David's failures.
And his adviser offered him a shortcut.
Do something shocking.
Make it public.
Force everyone to choose sides.
Make yourself impossible to ignore.
Does that sound entirely ancient?
We live in a world where public humiliation can become a form of influence.
Where people expose private wounds to win an argument.
Where families use secrets as weapons.
Where leaders confuse fear with respect.
Where someone may destroy another person's reputation simply to prove that they have power.
And where even religious people can become so obsessed with winning that they forget whom they are called to love.
Ahithophel's strategy was effective in its immediate political purpose.
But effectiveness is not righteousness.
Not every open door is from God.
Not every successful strategy has God's approval.
Not every influential voice deserves your obedience.
And not every adviser who knows how to strengthen your position knows how to protect your soul.
You can gain an audience and lose your integrity.
You can win a conflict and destroy your family.
You can appear powerful while becoming a prisoner of the very sin you used to obtain power.
Absalom entered Jerusalem as a conqueror.
But he was not free.
His ambition had become his master.
And before long, the rebellion would collapse.
In 2 Samuel 18, Absalom died during the conflict with David's forces.
When David heard the news, he cried:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (2 Samuel 18:33, KJV)
Stop there.
The son who publicly humiliated his father was dead.
The father whose kingdom had been threatened was weeping.
There was no celebration in David's cry.
Only grief.
A father mourning a son he could no longer reach.
A family devastated by sins that had multiplied across generations.
And a throne that could not bring back the dead.
That is the tragedy of Absalom.
He wanted his father's kingdom so desperately that he helped destroy the possibility of peace with his father.
And in the end, the kingdom he wanted could not save him.
But the Bible does not leave us with Absalom.
It leads us toward a greater King.
And this is where the story becomes more than a warning about political power.
Because centuries later, another Son of David would enter Jerusalem.
Not to seize a throne through sexual humiliation.
Not to strengthen His followers by making reconciliation impossible.
Not to sacrifice vulnerable people for His own advancement.
He came to give Himself.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The King whose kingdom is not established by exploiting others.
Listen to His own words:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Absalom used other people's humiliation to advance his claim to power.
Jesus willingly endured humiliation to save sinners.
Absalom sought to make himself king by taking.
Jesus revealed His kingship through sacrificial giving.
Absalom's rebellion fractured a household.
Christ came to reconcile sinners to God.
And on another day of public shame, the true King was stripped, mocked, and crucified.
He did not commit the sins for which He suffered.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve.
The cross was not another act of selfish royal ambition.
It was the place where the sinless Savior voluntarily laid down His life.
Philippians 2:8 declares:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
The world says power is proved by how many people you can make suffer for you.
Jesus reveals a kingdom in which the King suffers to redeem His people.
That is not weakness.
That is holy love.
And when Jesus rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin, shame, and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This does not mean every earthly wound instantly disappears.
It does not mean every family relationship will be restored in this life.
It does not mean that victims must return to unsafe situations or that repentance removes the need for justice.
It means something deeper.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Mercy is real.
And the crucified and risen Christ offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
Maybe you see yourself in David.
You have done things you wish you could undo.
You have hidden failures behind a respectable appearance.
You have asked God to forgive you, but you still struggle to face the truth about what happened.
Do not confuse concealment with healing.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Seek to make right what you can.
And trust the mercy of Jesus Christ, who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe you recognize something of Absalom in your own heart.
You have allowed pain to become bitterness.
You have justified cruelty because someone once treated you cruelly.
You have wanted revenge so badly that you stopped caring who would be hurt.
Your wounds matter.
But they do not give you permission to wound others.
Jesus calls you away from revenge and toward repentance.
Or perhaps you recognize the ten women.
You were not the person who started the conflict.
You were the person who suffered because of it.
You were treated like a possession.
Your voice was ignored.
Your dignity was sacrificed for someone else's ambition.
Hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not determine your worth before God.
You are not merely the worst thing that happened to you.
And the Gospel never asks you to call evil good.
Christ sees the afflicted, welcomes the burdened, and calls His people to protect the vulnerable and practice justice.
The same Savior who calls sinners to repentance also calls His followers to love their neighbors rather than exploit them.
That is why we must never read this passage only as a lesson about kings and thrones.
It is a warning about what happens when power is divorced from righteousness.
When ambition silences conscience.
When clever counsel replaces godly wisdom.
When a person's desire to win becomes greater than their willingness to obey God.
And when the people caught in the middle are forgotten.
The question is no longer simply, “Why did Ahithophel tell Absalom to sleep with his father's concubines?”
We know why.
He wanted a public demonstration of royal power.
He wanted to make Absalom's break with David unmistakable.
He wanted to strengthen the rebels by convincing them that reconciliation was no longer a realistic possibility.
The harder question is this:
What are you willing to sacrifice to get what your heart has decided it must have?
Your integrity?
Your marriage?
Your children?
Your conscience?
Your relationship with God?
Because the thing you are willing to sin to obtain can become the very thing that destroys you.
And no earthly throne is worth the loss of your soul.
Jesus asks in Mark 8:36:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (KJV)
Absalom gained Jerusalem for a moment.
But he lost far more than he understood.
Jesus offers something no stolen throne can provide.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new direction.
An eternal kingdom that cannot be overthrown.
And the invitation is not reserved for people whose stories are clean.
David's story was stained by adultery, abuse of power, deception, and bloodshed.
Yet Scripture also records his confession and God's mercy.
The point is not that sin becomes insignificant when God forgives.
The point is that God's grace is greater than the sinner's ability to save himself.
That is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Not because scandal is entertaining.
Not because brokenness makes a compelling headline.
But because Jesus Christ is the only Savior who can redeem sinners without denying the seriousness of their sin.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying shame for years.
You smile in church.
You encourage everyone else.
You know how to quote Scripture.
But there is something you have never brought honestly before God.
Or perhaps you are exhausted from trying to forgive someone who has never acknowledged the harm they caused.
You do not need to manufacture a testimony for an audience.
You need the truth.
You need the grace of Christ.
You need wise, faithful people who will help you walk in that truth.
And if your life has become a place of hidden sin, today is a good day to stop hiding.
Not because public exposure saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But because repentance begins with turning away from the lie that you can heal while continuing to protect what is destroying you.
And if God has been teaching you to release bitterness without excusing injustice, share what He has been showing you. Your testimony may help someone who feels alone.
We are not here to collect perfect religious answers.
We are here to point one another toward Jesus.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish dramatic Bible stories.
Not merely to attract attention.
But to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, recognize sin, discover the mercy of Christ, and grow into mature disciples who love God and love their neighbors.
Return to the Scriptures for yourself. Read 2 Samuel 11–20 and consider the whole narrative, not merely the scandal on the rooftop.
There is also a deeper way to stand alongside this ministry.
For Christians, generosity can be an expression of worship and gratitude to God. But it must always be willing, never pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
You can honor Christ through faithful stewardship, serving others, sharing biblical truth, supporting gospel work, and giving freely according to your ability and conviction.
That benefit is simply an expression of appreciation. The greater purpose is to strengthen biblical discipleship and make Christ-centered resources more accessible.
You are welcome to learn, grow, and share the truth whether or not you become a paying supporter.
Somebody is still trapped in shame.
Somebody is confusing religious performance with repentance.
Somebody has been wounded by a person who claimed to represent God.
Somebody thinks their past is too dark for forgiveness.
Somebody has never heard that the Son of David came not to exploit sinners, but to redeem them.
And somebody may encounter the Gospel because you chose to pass along the truth.
But never forget the center of the message.
It is not Absalom.
It is not Ahithophel.
It is not even David.
It is Jesus Christ.
The King who did not need to steal a throne.
The Savior who refused to use people as instruments of selfish ambition.
The Son of David who carried the cross, conquered the grave, and now calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
So do not leave this story merely horrified by an ancient scandal.
Leave it asking whether your own heart is being ruled by Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would be to recognize Absalom's ambition, condemn Ahithophel's counsel, grieve David's failures, and never surrender your own sin to the Savior.
The rooftop in Jerusalem reminds us how far sinful people will go to seize a kingdom.
The cross outside Jerusalem reveals how far the love of Christ went to redeem His people.
And there is one truth I hope stays with you long after you close this article:
Absalom tried to become king by making others bear his shame. Jesus proved Himself the true King by willingly bearing the shame of sinners to bring them home.
